title: The Only Claim Left in Court Was the Nursing Home's
description:
A family member of a patient requiring extensive nursing care signed an agreement with a nursing home, on behalf of the patient. Inside it was a clause requiring the parties to arbitrate all disputes, with one exception written into the same sentence: claims to collect late payments owed by the patient. The death claim went to a private arbitrator. The home's own bill stayed in a courthouse.

There were three negligence suits against West Virginia nursing homes, brought by Clayton Brown, Jeffrey Taylor and Sharon Marchio. In each case a patient had died and a family member sued, alleging that negligence caused injuries or harm resulting in death. The relevant parts of the agreements in Brown's case and Taylor's case were identical, and a state trial court dismissed both suits on those agreements. Marchio sued as executrix of the estate of Pauline Virginia Willett, the only patient the opinion names and only in the caption; her agreement was a different document, with no exceptions to the arbitration requirement at all and no mention of filing fees.

West Virginia's highest court then held unenforceable, as a matter of state public policy, every predispute arbitration agreement applying to a claim of personal injury or wrongful death against a nursing home. It considered whether the Federal Arbitration Act pre-empted that rule and decided it did not, calling the Supreme Court's reading of the Act tendentious and created from whole cloth.

On 21 February 2012 the Supreme Court answered in five pages, per curiam: no author's name on it and no vote reported. The statute's text includes no exception for personal-injury or wrongful-death claims. When state law prohibits outright the arbitration of a particular type of claim, the conflicting rule is displaced by the FAA. That rule resolves these cases. The judgment of the Supreme Court of Appeals of West Virginia was vacated and the cases were remanded.

That is the whole of what was decided, and it is less than the case is usually said to stand for. The Supreme Court did not hold that any of these three clauses was valid, and it ordered nobody to arbitrate anything. West Virginia had also called the clauses in Brown's and Taylor's cases unconscionable, and it was unclear how far that alternative holding had been influenced by the invalid categorical rule, so that question went back to be decided under state common law principles that are not specific to arbitration. As to Marchio's agreement, the state court had not addressed any ground other than public policy at all. And whether the relative who signs on behalf of a patient has the authority to sign anything away is a question this opinion never reaches.

West Virginia answered on 13 June 2012. In accordance with the mandate it overruled the syllabus point it had been reversed on, and otherwise reaffirmed its discussion and holdings, on the ground that the unconscionability doctrine it had built is a general, state, common-law, contract-law principle that is not specific to arbitration and does not implicate the FAA. It did not apply that doctrine to these clauses. One circuit court order was devoid of any findings of fact or conclusions of law on unconscionability and the other had never comprehensively analysed the question, so Brown's and Taylor's cases were reversed and remanded to the circuit courts for the taking of evidence. The argument that the family members who signed had no authority to sign, the court declined to consider, saying the trial court should consider it first.

Nothing in either opinion holds these clauses unenforceable, and nothing in either holds them enforceable. What the litigation settled was which sovereign's law governed a form signed at an admission desk, and almost nothing about whether the form was fair.

Some imagery in this film is AI-assisted and symbolic; no real-person likeness is shown, and no patient, injury or clinical scene is depicted.
Marmet Health Care Center, Inc. v. Brown, 565 U.S. 530 (2012) (per curiam).
